summary.text: Adelita Grijalva is the Democratic incumbent U.S. Representative for Arizona's 7th Congressional District. A Tucson native, she worked for more than 25 years at Pima County Teen Court, served on the Tucson Unified School District Governing Board from 2002 and on the Pima County Board of Supervisors from 2020, and won the seat in a September 2025 special election after the death of her father, Rep. Raúl Grijalva. She is seeking a full term in 2026.

paragraphs.text: Grijalva grew up with her two sisters on the south side of Tucson and graduated from Pueblo High School, according to her official House biography; Wikipedia gives the year as 1989.
She went on to earn a degree in political science from the University of Arizona, a B.A. in 1995 according to Wikipedia.
She then spent more than 25 years at Pima County Teen Court, serving as its director; the program is a restorative juvenile diversion program that helps court-involved youth and their families.

Grijalva was first elected to public office in 2002, to the Tucson Unified School District Governing Board. Her official bio says that as a volunteer board member she led an effort to expand preschool availability and defended Mexican-American Studies and bilingual curriculum against the state legislature. She served on the board for about 18 years, and according to Wikipedia she was the only board member to vote against ending the district's Mexican American Studies classes in 2012.
In 2020 she was elected to the Pima County Board of Supervisors, where she became the first Latina, and the second woman, to chair the board.
Her office lists among her accomplishments there a county free preschool program for low- and middle-income families, investments in affordable housing, and the protection of open space.
Grijalva is the daughter of Rep. Raúl Grijalva, who died on March 13, 2025. She won his seat in the September 23, 2025 special election, defeating Republican Daniel Butierez Sr. 68.9% to 29.4%.
Although she won the election on September 23, she was not sworn in until November 12, 2025, about 50 days later, when the House returned from a recess during the federal government shutdown.

She serves on the House Committee on Education and Workforce and the Committee on Natural Resources, and her office lists memberships in caucuses including the Congressional Progressive Caucus and the Congressional Hispanic Caucus.
She lives in Tucson with her husband Sol and has three children, according to her official bio.
